sections.b: Mark 4 is Mark's only long collection of parables: the sower (4:3–9), the explanation of why Jesus speaks in parables (4:10–12, quoting Isaiah 6:9–10), the sower explained (4:13–20), the sayings on the lamp and the measure (4:21–25), the seed that grows by itself, found only in Mark (4:26–29), and the mustard seed (4:30–32). Jesus speaks from a boat to a crowd on the shore, then explains in private. Mark frames the whole with the call to hear (4:3, 9, 23–24) and says Jesus spoke to the crowds only in parables but explained everything to his disciples privately (4:33–34). Mary Ann Tolbert read the sower as the key to Mark's whole story, with the disciples as the rocky ground.

common: The sower, the lamp and the mustard seed appear in Matthew and Luke too; the seed that grows by itself is in Mark alone.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that "so that" in Mark 4:12 means "so that Scripture is fulfilled," or that its last clause means "unless they turn," not that Jesus meant to hide the truth.

sections.b: Mark's three seed parables picture God's kingdom as hidden and small now, certain and great later. The sower's seed is mostly lost, yet the good soil yields thirty, sixty and a hundredfold (Mark 4:8). The seed sown by a farmer who then sleeps grows "on its own," and when the grain is ripe he sends in the sickle, an echo of Joel's harvest of judgment (Mark 4:26–29; Joel 3:13). The mustard seed, the proverbial smallest seed, becomes a plant where the birds of the sky shelter, as in the Old Testament's pictures of great kingdoms as trees (Mark 4:30–32; Daniel 4:12; Ezekiel 17:23). Mark calls it "the mystery of the kingdom of God" (Mark 4:11), given to those who come close.
sections.refs: Mark 4:11; Mark 4:26–32; Joel 3:13; Daniel 4:12; Ezekiel 17:22–24; Matthew 13:31–33

sections.b: After the parables Mark tells four great miracles in a row: the stilling of the storm (Mark 4:35–41), the freeing of the man with the legion (Mark 5:1–20), the healing of the woman with a flow of blood and the raising of Jairus' daughter (Mark 5:21–43). Together they show Jesus' power over nature, demons, sickness and death. Each ends with fear or amazement, and the disciples' question, "Who can this be?" (Mark 4:41), runs through them. In Nazareth, by contrast, Jesus "was not able to do any act of power" because of unbelief (Mark 6:5), which Matthew softens (Matthew 13:58). The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle told in all four Gospels (Mark 6:30–44; John 6:1–15).

uncommon: Ched Myers and others read the drowning of the "Legion" in the sea as a picture of Roman power driven out of the land.

sections.b: On the Gentile shore a man lives among the tombs, held by spirits that call themselves "Legion is my name, because there are a lot of us" (Mark 5:9), using the Latin word for a Roman army unit. They bow before Jesus, try to bind him with an exorcist's oath "by God," beg not to be sent out of the region, and ask to enter a herd of pigs, which then rushes into the sea (Mark 5:1–13). Mark does not explain where demons come from; he shows them knowing who Jesus is ("Son of God Most High," Mark 5:7) and powerless before him. Modern readers differ on how possession relates to mental illness; Mark's point is that the man is restored to his right mind (Mark 5:15).

Mark tells two sea miracles. In the storm, Jesus sleeps on the cushion, then "spoke sternly" to the wind and told the sea, "Be muzzled!" (Mark 4:39). The Greek verb behind "spoke sternly," epitimaō, is the one Mark uses when Jesus silences demons (Mark 1:25; Mark 3:12; Mark 9:25; compare Mark 8:30, 32, 33), though the English there reads "strict order" or "rebuked," and "Be muzzled" is his word to a demon in Mark 1:25. The disciples ask who this is that the wind and sea obey (Mark 4:35–41). In the Psalms only the LORD does this (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:29). Later he comes to the disciples walking on the sea, meaning to "pass by" them, and says "I am" (Mark 6:45–52), language the Old Testament uses of God, who "tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8) and passes by Moses and Elijah (Exodus 34:6; 1 Kings 19:11).
sections.refs: Mark 1:25; Mark 3:12; Mark 4:35–41; Mark 6:45–52; Mark 9:25; Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:23–30; Job 9:8–11; Exodus 34:6; 1 Kings 19:11; Jonah 1:4–16

sections.h: Herod Antipas and Herodias in Mark
sections.b: Mark calls Herod Antipas "King Herod" (Mark 6:14), though he was a tetrarch, as Matthew 14:1 and Luke 9:7 say. Mark tells how Antipas imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, the wife of his brother, how Herod both feared and protected John, and how Herodias used her daughter's dance and Herod's oath at his birthday banquet to have John beheaded (Mark 6:17–29). Mark names Herodias' first husband "Philip"; Josephus names him Herod and says Salome, her daughter, married Philip the tetrarch. The manuscripts of Mark 6:22 differ on whether the dancer is "his daughter Herodias" or "the daughter of Herodias herself." Josephus adds that Antipas killed John at Machaerus for fear of an uprising, and that Herodias' ambition later led to Antipas' exile.

Mark's account of John's death (Mark 6:14–29) is the only story in his Gospel not centered on Jesus. It is told as a flashback inside the mission of the Twelve, so that the disciples' preaching is framed by a martyrdom. Mark casts John as Elijah and Herodias as a new Jezebel, and he ends with John's disciples laying his body in a tomb, as Joseph of Arimathea will lay Jesus' body (Mark 15:46). Mark calls John both "the Baptizer" (Mark 1:4; 6:14, 24) and "the Baptist" (Mark 6:25; 8:28). Josephus confirms the execution (Antiquities 18.116–119).

In Nazareth the people call Jesus "the builder ... the son of Mary, and the brother of James, Joses, Judas and Simon," and mention his sisters (Mark 6:3). Only Mark has "son of Mary" without naming Joseph; readers explain this by Joseph's death, by Mark's silence about a human father, or, as some have argued, by a slur on Jesus' birth. Mark 15:40 names a Mary who was mother of James the younger and of Joses; Jerome and the Catholic Catechism (500) take her to be a different Mary, so that the "brothers" were relatives. Others read Mark 6:3 as naming Mary's own sons. See the card at Mark 6.
sections.refs: Mark 3:31–35; Mark 6:3; Mark 15:40; Mark 15:47; Matthew 13:55–56; Matthew 27:56

sections.b: Mark tells Jesus' return to his hometown, which he does not name here (Mark 1:9 does). In the synagogue on the Sabbath the people are stunned by his wisdom and acts of power but are tripped up because they know him as the local builder and his family. Jesus answers with the proverb that a prophet is honored everywhere except at home, and Mark says frankly that he "was not able to do any act of power there" except heal a few sick people, and that their unbelief astonished him. Matthew 13:58 softens this; Luke 4:16–30 tells a fuller and more violent scene at the start of Jesus' ministry.

Only Mark says that the Twelve, on their first mission, anointed many of the sick with oil and healed them (Mark 6:13). Olive oil was a common medicine (Isaiah 1:6; Luke 10:34), but here it goes with the authority Jesus gave them. James 5:14–15 tells church elders to pray over the sick and anoint them in the Lord's name. The Council of Trent named Mark 6:13 as a hint of the sacrament of the anointing of the sick; Orthodox churches keep Holy Unction; many Protestants anoint with prayer without calling it a sacrament. See the card at Mark 6.

Jesus had appointed the Twelve "to be with him" and to be sent out (Mark 3:14). In Mark 6:7–13 he sends them two by two with authority over unclean spirits, taking only a staff and sandals, no bread, bag or money, and telling them to stay in one house and to shake off the dust of towns that reject them. They preach repentance, drive out demons and anoint the sick. On their return Mark calls them "the apostles" (Mark 6:30), the only time he uses the word, in its plain sense: the ones who were sent. Matthew 10 and Luke 9 give longer versions of the instructions; Matthew and Luke forbid the staff that Mark allows.

When Jesus sees the crowd, "his heart went out to them, for they were like sheep that have no shepherd" (Mark 6:34), the words of Moses' prayer for a leader (Numbers 27:17) and Micaiah's vision (1 Kings 22:17). Ezekiel 34 promised that God himself would shepherd his flock. Jesus first teaches them, then has them recline on the green grass, as in Psalm 23:2, and feeds them all. Mark's picture is of the promised shepherd gathering Israel in the wilderness.
sections.refs: Mark 6:34–44; Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5–23; Psalm 23:1–2; Mark 14:27

sections.b: John's Gospel is not the only one with an "I am" that may echo God's name. In Mark 6:50, walking on the sea and meaning to "pass by" the disciples, Jesus says, "Courage! I am. Stop being afraid." The Greek egō eimi can simply mean "It's me," but in this setting many scholars hear the divine "I am" of Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10. Mark uses it again in Jesus' answer to the high priest (Mark 14:62), and Jesus warns of others who will come saying "I am" (Mark 13:6). Matthew 14:27 and John 6:20 have the same words in the same scene.
sections.refs: Mark 6:50; Mark 13:6; Mark 14:62; Matthew 14:27; John 6:20; Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10

sections.b: Mark applies the language of hardening not only to outsiders but to Jesus' own disciples. The parables are given to outsiders so that, in Isaiah's words, they look and do not see (Mark 4:11–12). Yet after the walk on the sea Mark says the disciples "had not grasped what the loaves meant. Instead, their hearts had turned hard" (Mark 6:52), the word used of Jesus' opponents in Mark 3:5, and Jesus asks them, "Have your hearts turned hard?" (Mark 8:17), quoting the same Isaiah passage back to them. Matthew's parallel ends instead with the disciples bowing down before Jesus (Matthew 14:33).
sections.refs: Mark 3:5; Mark 4:11–12; Mark 6:52; Mark 8:17–21; Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 14:33

sections.b: The woman with the flow of blood touches Jesus' cloak, which Matthew and Luke specify as its tassel (Mark 5:27; Matthew 9:20; Luke 8:44). At Gennesaret the sick plead to touch "even the tassel of his cloak," and all who touch him are saved (Mark 6:56). The tassel (kraspedon) is the fringe commanded in Numbers 15:38. That Jesus wore one shows him as an observant Jew; older English Bibles hid it as the "hem" of his garment.

Mark 5 moves through the main sources of impurity in Jewish law: a Gentile region, tombs and an unclean spirit (Mark 5:1–5), pigs (Leviticus 11:7), a woman with a flow of blood (Leviticus 15:25–27) and a corpse (Numbers 19:11). In each case the uncleanness gives way to Jesus. Christian readers have often said Jesus broke purity laws here. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine and Paula Fredriksen reply that the text never says so: the woman was not forbidden to be in a crowd or to touch, and impurity was not sin. Mark's emphasis is on healing and faith.

Mark keeps several of Jesus' Aramaic words and translates them: "Talitha koum," "Little girl, I tell you, get up" (Mark 5:41), as well as Boanerges (Mark 3:17), korban (Mark 7:11), ephphatha (Mark 7:34), Abba (Mark 14:36) and the cry from the cross (Mark 15:34). The habit shows that Jesus spoke Aramaic and that Mark wrote for readers who did not. The later manuscripts' "koumi" corrects the grammar to the feminine form.
sections.refs: Mark 3:17; Mark 5:41; Mark 7:11; Mark 7:34; Mark 14:36; Mark 15:34

sections.b: In Mark the opposite of faith is fear. After the storm Jesus asks, "Why are you timid? You still don't have faith?" (Mark 4:40). The woman comes "frightened and shaking," but Jesus says her faith has saved her (Mark 5:33–34). Jairus, told his daughter has died, hears, "Stop being afraid. Just keep believing" (Mark 5:36). In Nazareth unbelief blocks Jesus' acts of power (Mark 6:5–6). The Gospel's last words describe the women at the tomb as afraid (Mark 16:8), leaving the reader to choose.

Mark's feeding of the five thousand takes place in a "lonely" or wilderness place (Mark 6:31–35), with the crowd arranged in hundreds and fifties like Israel under Moses (Exodus 18:21) and fed until full, with twelve baskets left over. Many readers hear the manna (Exodus 16) and the psalmist's question whether God can lay out a table in the wilderness (Psalm 78:19). Mark later says the disciples did not understand "the loaves" (Mark 6:52; 8:14–21).
sections.refs: Mark 6:30–44; Mark 6:52; Mark 8:1–21; Exodus 16; Exodus 18:21; Psalm 78:19–25; 2 Kings 4:42–44; John 6:1–15

sections.b: Mark 4–6 supplies several standard examples used in the Synoptic debate. Mark's disciples rebuke Jesus, "Teacher ... doesn't it matter to you that we are going down?" (Mark 4:38); Matthew and Luke turn it into a plea. Mark says Jesus "was not able" to do acts of power in Nazareth (Mark 6:5); Matthew says he "did not do many" (Matthew 13:58). Mark says the disciples' hearts were hardened (Mark 6:52); Matthew has them bow down before Jesus (Matthew 14:33). Mark has the doctors make the woman worse (Mark 5:26), which Matthew omits and Luke softens. Most scholars think such changes are easier to explain if Matthew and Luke used Mark than the reverse.
sections.refs: Mark 4:38; Mark 5:26; Mark 6:5; Mark 6:52; Matthew 8:25; Matthew 13:58; Matthew 14:33; Luke 8:24; Luke 8:43

sections.b: In Mark 5–6 healing comes through touch: Jairus asks Jesus to lay his hands on his daughter, a woman touches Jesus' cloak and power goes out of him, Jesus takes the dead girl's hand, he lays his hands on a few sick people in Nazareth, and at Gennesaret all who touch even his tassel are saved (Mark 5:23–41; Mark 6:5, 56). His disciples anoint the sick with oil (Mark 6:13). Mark uses the verb "save" for these healings, so that bodily healing and salvation are heard together (Mark 5:23, 28, 34; Mark 6:56).

Jesus invites his apostles to rest in a "lonely spot," literally a wilderness place (Mark 6:31–32), the setting where John preached and Jesus was tested (Mark 1:3–13). There the crowd is fed like Israel in the wilderness, arranged in hundreds and fifties and given bread from heaven's hand (Mark 6:35–44).

Mark sets Herod's birthday banquet for the powerful, which ends with a prophet's head on a platter (Mark 6:21–28), right before Jesus' meal for the poor in the wilderness, where the crowd reclines "party by party" (symposia) on the green grass and eats until full (Mark 6:39–44). Many readers see in the second a foretaste of the feast God promised for the end of the age (Isaiah 25:6).

sections.h: John, Herod and Herodias as Elijah, Ahab and Jezebel
sections.b: Mark tells John's death so that it echoes Elijah's struggle with Ahab and Jezebel: a weak king who respects the prophet, a queen who wants him dead (1 Kings 19:2; 1 Kings 21), and a prophet who condemns the royal household. Some people thought Jesus himself was Elijah (Mark 6:15; 8:28), but Mark's Jesus says Elijah has already come and was treated any way they pleased (Mark 9:11–13), meaning John.
sections.refs: Mark 6:14–29; Mark 6:15; Mark 8:28; Mark 9:11–13; 1 Kings 19:1–2; 1 Kings 21:1–16; Malachi 4:5

sections.b: Mark 4–6 shows several of Mark's habits at once. The parables chapter (Mark 4:1–34) draws a line between insiders and "those outside" and then shows the insiders failing to understand. A run of boat crossings over the Sea of Galilee (Mark 4:35; 5:21; 6:32, 45, 53) takes Jesus back and forth between Jewish and Gentile shores. Two of Mark's "sandwiches" sit here: the bleeding woman inside Jairus' story (Mark 5:21–43) and John's death inside the mission of the Twelve (Mark 6:7–30). Orders of silence (Mark 5:43) alternate with a command to tell (Mark 5:19). And Mark's frankness, which Matthew and Luke soften, shows clearly: the disciples rebuke Jesus (Mark 4:38), Jesus "was not able" to do acts of power in Nazareth (Mark 6:5), and the disciples' hearts turn hard (Mark 6:52).
sections.refs: Mark 4:1–6:56; Mark 4:11; Mark 4:38; Mark 5:19; Mark 5:21–43; Mark 5:43; Mark 6:5; Mark 6:7–30; Mark 6:52
